claims.text: The base HfNbTaTiZr alloy is equimolar, with approximately 20 at.% of each element.
The proposed application includes bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model will use ab initio oxygen-scattering cross sections, defect concentrations, and temperature-dependent electron–phonon-coupling modifications as input features.
The prediction is intended to cover 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Oxygen impurities and associated defect states introduce additional electron-scattering channels in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen impurities and associated defects modify the electron mean free path.
Learning from electron–phonon and oxygen/defect scattering rates will allow the model to adjust effective electron transport separately with temperature.
Perfect-crystal assumptions cause systematic deviations in conductivity predictions for real HfNbTaTiZr.
Accounting for microstructural disorder and impurities will make predictions track experimental conductivity more closely.
The machine-learning framework will be significantly more accurate than traditional defect-free analytical models.
The model will have smaller conductivity-prediction errors across both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
A specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen will have lower conductivity than the ideal defect-free state because of increased electron scattering.
Existing analytical approaches assume perfect, defect-free crystals and neglect oxygen-induced scattering.
Existing analytical approaches systematically overestimate conductivity when impurities are present.
The approach is expected to apply to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen concentrations up to about 1 wt.%.
Applicability outside 0–200 K and 300–1200 K or at substantially different oxygen concentrations is uncertain.
Prediction accuracy depends on the quality and representativeness of the ab initio inputs and experimental training data.
A held-out temperature such as 150 K or 800 K will be used to test predictive generalization.
The hypothesis is falsified if the oxygen-containing specimen's prediction error exceeds that of defect-free analytical models by a statistically significant amount.
